column4: This ayah describes trained hunting animals catching wild game for their human handlers; it puts the section's tamed animal and its unowned wild herds into one specific scene.
One ant warns the other ants to enter their homes, giving the section's bee leader and following group a direct animal parallel of a guide directing its community.
Moses asks to follow a teacher who can guide him; this makes explicit the follower's request for a leader that the section draws from the herd's fore-animal.
God says whoever follows His guidance will not go astray; this joins the section's image of a lost animal and a follower needing a guide in one claim.
This ayah says those who follow God's guidance need not fear or grieve; it makes following guidance the answer to the section's image of the lost and the led.
This ayah names the she-camel given to Thamud as a clear sign and says they wronged it; it adds another Qur'anic camel scene in which human treatment of the animal is decisive.
This ayah says every people has a guide; its guide (root ه د ي) parallels the source's dictionary form hādī for the animal going ahead of a group.
The ayah asks people to look at how camels were created; it directs attention to the same animal whose carrying body, mark, and domestication the section examines.
Solomon's human, jinn, and bird forces are gathered in ranks; this supplies a Qur'anic scene of a leader arranging a group that includes animals.
Solomon checks the birds and notices the hoopoe is missing; this is a specific scene of an animal absent from its leader's ordered company.
The hoopoe returns with news after being missing in 27:20; its own contribution is the animal's return to the leader, completing the loss-and-return scene.
The fish slips away into the sea during a journey; it parallels the section's camel escaping its owner, while the fish's purposeful route contrasts with the camel left ownerless.
The companion admits forgetting the fish and reports that it went into the sea; this ayah supplies the remembered loss that leads to the return in 18:64.
Moses recognizes the fish's disappearance as what they sought and turns back; this ayah completes the search around an escaped animal.
This ayah describes people assigning portions of crops and livestock to God and their partners; it adds a contested claim of ownership to the section's marked herd and unknown owner.
For killed wild game, this ayah prescribes an equivalent from domestic livestock; it explicitly sets wild animals beside managed herd animals.
This ayah distinguishes lawful sea game from land game forbidden during consecration; it marks a boundary between wild animals and the managed animals in the section.
God appoints Abraham an imam for people; the leader (imam) is a human counterpart to the source's dictionary forms for the herd animal that goes ahead.
The prophet appoints Talut as king over his people; the human ruler named malik gives a specific follower-and-leader counterpart to the source's dictionary form for the herd's leading animal.

A king's cup is reported lost, and its finder is promised a camel-load; the verse gives a concrete lost-property scene whose reward is measured through a camel, contrasting with the section's camel lost from its owner.
The Qur'anic mark (root و س م) identifies discreet poor people; unlike the source's camel brand that identifies an owner, this mark reveals the person's condition.
People on the barrier recognize others by their marks (root و س م); the identifying sign parallels the source's camel brand but signals a person's standing.
The ayah says hypocrites can be recognized by their marks (root و س م); this is another human-status use of the identifying-mark root named for the camel brand.
The ayah describes a mark on believers' faces (root و س م); the sign parallels the source's identifying camel brand while marking devotion rather than ownership.
The criminals are recognized by their marks (root و س م); as with the camel brand, a visible sign identifies its bearer, though here it signals guilt.
The parable contrasts one person divided among quarrelsome owners with one belonging to a single owner; it illuminates the section's statement that a herd has a master.

This ayah contrasts an owned, powerless servant with a person provided for; the servant word shares root ع ب د with the source's dictionary form muʿabbad for the subdued camel, while showing the human sense of that root.
The leaders admit that they led their followers astray; it reverses the section's good herd-leader who guides those behind him.
